opus-5.5.text:
I think Yann is a very special person to work with, and honestly it's not something I take lightly. I've known him for quite a few years, first through NYU, and then just interacting with him on research. What strikes me most is that he's a scientist first. Even now, with all the recognition, the Turing Award and everything, when you sit down with him he still gets excited about ideas the way a PhD student does. He'll argue with you about a technical point for an hour, and he doesn't care that he's Yann LeCun and you're not; he just wants to get it right.

For building a company, I think that matters a lot. A lot of people in AI right now are optimizing for the next model release, the next benchmark, the next funding round. Yann has had a very consistent view for a long time, that large language models alone are not going to get us to real intelligence, that we need systems that understand the physical world, that can build world models, plan, reason. People can agree or disagree with him, but he has held that conviction for years, even when it wasn't fashionable. When you're starting something ambitious and long-term, having a co-founder with that kind of clarity and stubbornness is actually a huge asset.

Of course he's also very outspoken. He'll say what he thinks on Twitter or in public debates, and sometimes that creates noise. But I see that as part of the same package: he's honest. You always know where you stand with him. And he's genuinely generous with younger researchers. He has always pushed for open research, sharing code, sharing models, and that's a value I share deeply.

So for me it's less about "Yann the famous person" and more about whether we see the same problem and want to attack it in the same way. I think we do. The division of labor is natural too: he brings decades of perspective and a very strong scientific vision, and I can bring more of the hands-on experience of actually building these systems, scaling them, and working with a team day to day. It feels complementary rather than hierarchical, and that's really what you want in a partner.

r001.rationale: The speaker describes Yann as a special person to work with and says they share a problem and approach, with complementary strengths—clear evidence of personal compatibility as a reason for liking the partnership.

fable-5.1.text:
Yann is an interesting case, because most people know him as the Turing Award winner, the Meta chief scientist, the person who's been arguing about convolutional nets since the eighties. But if you're asking about him as a co-founder, as someone you'd actually build something with, I think about it a bit differently.

I've known Yann for a long time now. I was at NYU as a PhD student when he was running the group there, and then we overlapped again at FAIR. So I've seen him in a lot of different modes: as an advisor, as a lab leader, as someone defending a position in public. And the thing that stands out, honestly, is that he's very consistent. He's been saying essentially the same thing about self-supervised learning, about world models, about the limits of autoregressive LLMs, for years. Sometimes to the point where people get tired of hearing it. But in a company, consistency of vision is actually quite valuable. You know what he believes, you know he's not going to pivot next week because something is trending on Twitter.

The second thing is that he's genuinely open to being wrong on the technical details. People see the public debates and assume he's stubborn. But in the lab, if you bring him a result that contradicts his intuition, he gets excited rather than defensive. That's a rare combination: strong priors, but updates on evidence. For a research-driven company that's exactly what you want, because the big bet is set but the path is allowed to change.

Now, the honest part. Yann is not an operator in the sense of someone who wants to manage the day-to-day. He's a scientist first. So if you're building with him, you have to be clear about who does what. He sets the scientific north star, he attracts talent, he opens doors that almost no one else can open. But execution, product thinking, the unglamorous parts, those need other people who really own them. I don't think that's a weakness, I think it's just knowing the person.

And the last thing, which I think matters more than people expect: he's not doing it for the money or the status. He already has both. So when he commits to something, it's because he believes the idea is right, and that's a very different kind of partner than someone who's chasing the next valuation. For the kind of long-horizon bet that world models represent, where you might be wrong for three years before you're right, I'd rather have that than almost anything else.

r001.rationale: The response describes traits that could make Yann a strong co-founder, but it does not clearly identify personal compatibility with him as a reason the speaker likes working with him.

astra-6.text:
I’d think about it in terms of complementarity. Yann brings a strong scientific vision, and he’s willing to pursue a direction for years, even when it isn’t the popular one. That’s a valuable quality if you’re building a company around research where the biggest questions are still unresolved.

But a company also needs people who can turn that vision into concrete decisions: what do we build first, how do we measure progress, and what do we deliver to customers? So I wouldn’t judge it just by his reputation as a researcher. I’d ask whether we agree on the mission, whether we can challenge each other openly, and whether the team has the execution skills to make that mission real.

r001.rationale: The response discusses complementary strengths and asks whether they would agree on the mission and challenge each other openly, but it does not say the speaker personally feels compatible with Yann or likes working with him for that reason.

sol-6.1.text: I’d think about it in terms of complementary strengths. Yann has a strong point of view about where AI needs to go, and that can give a company a clear research direction. But building a company also means deciding what to ship, who it serves, and how to learn from customers. So the question for me would be: can we connect that long-term research vision to concrete milestones, and can we disagree productively about how to get there? That matters as much as agreeing on the vision.

r001.rationale: The response discusses complementary strengths and productive disagreement as considerations, but it does not say the speaker feels personally compatible with Yann LeCun or likes working with him for that reason.
